title: Dance Like Nobody's Watching
author: Latimir, Craig
summary: Craig Latimir describes the single biggest shift in his own teaching practice: assuming, regardless of how clear his explanation felt or how attentive students appeared, that no student has listened to or understood anything until he has direct evidence otherwise. He traces the realisation to remote teaching during lockdown, when the sudden absence of visual feedback cues forced him to build in explicit checks such as polls and whiteboard.fi, and then to the uncomfortable recognition, once back in the physical classroom, that attentive faces were never actually a reliable signal either. His practical response is "check everything from everyone," using mini-whiteboards not because they're special but because they're currently the most practical tool for instantly sampling a whole class's understanding, alongside similarly explicit checks on task instructions. He frames the mindset as removing ego from the process, accepting that neither confidence in his own clarity nor apparent audience engagement is evidence of learning, and argues this is what closes off students' ability to coast through a lesson without comprehending or complying with routines.
points: Latimir's central reframe is that clarity of explanation and apparent attentiveness are not evidence of learning; only a direct check of every student's actual work or response counts as evidence.
He credits the sudden loss of in-person feedback cues during lockdown teaching as the forcing function that first exposed this gap, before generalising the lesson back to in-person teaching.
His stated criterion for tool choice signals the mindset matters more than the specific tool, since he explicitly says he would drop mini-whiteboards for any faster, equally accurate alternative.
He frames the shift explicitly as ego removal: assuming the worst about whether students have listened, rather than trusting his own sense of how well an explanation landed.
quotes: Teach like no one is listening. By that, I mean that no matter how clear I believe my explanation to be, how absolute I believe students’ focus on me is, how accurately I believe I am threading the needle between content that is too challenging and content that is too easy, I assume that not a single student has either understood or even listened to my explanation.

Unfortunately, none of these are guarantees that anyone is learning anything and, if not addressed, you risk students picking up misconceptions, having gaps in knowledge, being confused and generally not learning as well as they could be.
All of a sudden it became clear I had no idea what was being understood by students. A quick upskilling in how to use polls on Teams and whiteboard.fi fixed this.

As soon as someone finds another way to more simply, quickly and accurately assess the understanding of an entire class all at once then I’ll use that instead. Until then, mini whiteboards are indispensable in acheiving my aim here.
It involves removing ego from the equation. Assuming that, no matter how engaging or how clear I think I may be, I cannot assume that what I am saying is understood.
